# How I'll manage my land this year

Let me think about this the way I always do. I've been farming this piece of land for thirty years now, so I know what it likes and what it gives back.

## My fields

I have 7 mu total. Most of it — about 5 mu — is my wheat-maize land, the good flat land near the road. The other 2 mu is sandier, that's where I plant peanuts. Peanuts don't like the heavy soil, and my mother-in-law always said that piece was better for peanuts, so that's what I do. My husband and I set it up this way years ago.

## Wheat (5 mu)

I plant after the maize is cleared, around the beginning of October, same as everyone in the village. I buy seed from the agricultural store in town — the usual wheat they sell, I don't know the name of it but the shopkeeper gives me what he gives the others. I sow a bit thick because some always fails.

For fertilizer, I put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu before the planter goes. That's the red-and-white bag — the one with three numbers on it. I know it from the color. Then in the spring when the wheat wakes up and starts shooting up, I broadcast urea on top, about half a bag per mu. My neighbor Old Wang does the same, maybe a little more, but he has a bigger family eating the flour so he pushes harder.

I'll irrigate three times if the sky doesn't help me — once before winter when the ground freezes, once at jointing in spring, and once when the grain is filling. Each time costs money for the pump and the electricity. If it rains, I skip one. Last year it rained in April so I only pumped twice.

For spraying, my son-in-law comes with the sprayer on his back when the weeds come up. I use the cheap weed killer. If I see aphids I spray once more.

I'm hoping for 400 kg per mu. If the wheat is good I'll get 450, if it's a bad year maybe only 350. I've seen both.

## Maize (5 mu, after the wheat)

Right after the wheat comes off in June, we have to move fast. The village combine takes the wheat one day, and within the week the maize has to be in the ground. No time to plow properly — we just use the no-till planter that the village cooperative rents out. Puts the maize seed right in through the wheat stubble.

I buy hybrid maize seed — the one everyone plants here. My second son brings it from the store. The compound fertilizer goes in with the seed — about one bag per mu — and later when the maize is up to my knee I side-dress urea, maybe 15 kg per mu, pushing it in near the plants.

Usually I don't need to irrigate maize — summer rains take care of it. But if July and August are dry, I'll pump once or twice. I watch the corn leaves — if they start to curl, I pump.

I spray once for weeds after planting, and watch for armyworm. If I see them eating the leaves I spray.

I'm expecting maybe 450 kg per mu. The summer maize here is pretty reliable if the rains come.

## Peanut (2 mu)

I plant peanuts in late April or early May when the soil is warm. I saved some seed from last year — good peanuts, I picked out the plumpest ones. But I'll also buy a little new seed to mix in because my daughter-in-law says too many years of own-seed makes the yield go down.

Peanuts don't need much fertilizer — they make their own, my father taught me that long ago. I just put one bag of compound per mu at planting, that's it. No topdressing.

I'll cover the rows with plastic film — this makes a big difference for peanuts here, keeps the soil warm and holds moisture. It costs money and it's a pain to lay, but the yield is much better with it.

I irrigate once or twice if May is dry. Peanuts need water when they're flowering and making pods.

Peanut is more work than grain. When harvest comes in September, the whole family helps — my two daughters come back from the city for a few days. We pull the plants, knock off the soil, and lay them out to dry. If we don't have enough hands, I hire a neighbor woman for a few days.

I'm hoping for 280 kg per mu of peanut. Last year I got 300, year before only 230 because of the dry spell.

## What worries me

Fertilizer prices have been going up. A bag of urea costs more than it used to. I'd like to put more on but I have to watch what I spend — there's still the electricity bill, and my granddaughter needs school supplies. My eldest son sends money home from the construction site but I don't like to depend on it.

If it's a dry year I'll have bigger pumping costs for the wheat irrigation. That's always on my mind in the spring.
